01

Intelligent Knee Rehabilitation Device

Independent STEM Research — Charter School of Wilmington, 2024

Post-operative knee recovery is slow, inconsistent, and hard to measure — so I built a device to fix that.

I designed and built a mechanized, sensor-instrumented rehabilitation device that moves the knee joint through a controlled, repeatable range of motion, aiming to make recovery faster, more measurable, and more consistent than unsupervised physical therapy.

The problem

  • 200,000+ ACL injuries occur in the U.S. each year (Musahl & Karlsson, 2019), and the AAOS projects 3.5 million knee surgeries annually by 2030.
  • Roughly 50% of patients don't consistently follow prescribed home exercises (Argent et al., 2018) — traditional rehab has low compliance and is hard to access.

How I built it

The device uses linear actuators and an Arduino Mega to drive the knee joint through a controlled, repeatable range of motion, tracking ROM, speed, and force in real time with visual feedback through custom software I wrote. I modeled every mechanical component in Onshape, designed the control electronics in Altium Designer, and 3D-printed functional prototypes through several iterations to refine actuator placement and comfort. To test it, I ran a device-assisted group against a control group performing the same exercises unassisted.

Results

118.2° vs 105.9°
Range of motion — device-assisted vs. control group
6.5s vs 8.0s
Time per repetition — device-assisted vs. control group

The results supported both hypotheses: the device improved knee function and, by structuring the exercise, improved adherence — earning 1st Place at the state science fair and an invitation to the NESTEC Blue Apple conference.

02

Autonomous Object Detection & Environment Mapping

Independent STEM Research — Charter School of Wilmington, 2023

Self-driving cars live or die by their sensors — I wanted to find out which one actually works for real-time mapping.

I built and benchmarked a four-wheeled robotic platform to compare five distance sensors — ultrasonic, RPLidar A1, TF-Mini S Lidar, Time-of-Flight, and Sharp IR — to determine which is best suited for real-time 2D environment mapping, motivated by the sensing needs of self-driving cars.

The question

I set out to test the null hypothesis that no sensor is superior to the others in maximum detection distance or 2D-mapping quality — a real trade-off in cost, range, and accuracy that any autonomous platform has to make.

How I tested it

I assembled a mobile robot platform (motors, wheels, battery pack, Arduino Uno + motor shield), wrote and uploaded Arduino code for each sensor, then ran 10 trials per sensor in a gymnasium, recording distance readings and generating 2D surroundings maps with the RPLidar A1.

4.4 / 5
RPLidar A1 mapping-quality score (σ = 0.63) — every other sensor scored 0
p ≈ 2.76×10⁻⁸
Statistical significance, Ultrasonic vs. TF-Mini S Lidar

The data rejected the null hypothesis: RPLidar's 360° rotating scan proved superior for 2D mapping, consistent with prior published research (Akhil & Chandan, 2022) showing LiDAR outperforms ultrasonic for complex structure measurement — winning 1st Place at the county science fair and a $500 national GripTape Grant.

03

Clean Hydrogen Project

Electrical Design Leader — Partnered with University of Delaware, 2024–2025

I turned a clean-energy hardware concept into a real product schools could actually buy and use.

I founded and led the electrical design and PCB layout for a hydrogen-electrolyzer teaching device, taking it from a rough concept all the way through prototyping and validation to a sellable product now in use at approximately 20 high schools.

How I built it

I designed the control electronics in Altium Designer and built the panel around a water-electrolyzer cell that splits H₂O into hydrogen and oxygen, with a labeled front panel — power switch, H₂O pump control, and electric power control — so anyone could operate it safely. I also 3D-printed the mounting brackets and enclosures for the pump and gas-collection tank, iterating through several prototype revisions to get the wiring and fit right.

From prototype to product

The panel went through a full visual and functional overhaul between early builds and the finished unit — clearer labeling, tidier wiring, and a more durable mount — the kind of iteration that comes from actually handing the device to teachers and students and seeing what needed to change.

~20 Schools
High schools using the finished device in a paid product role · 2024–2025
4 Stages
Concept → PCB design → 3D-printed enclosure → shipped product

Beyond the engineering, I managed the commercial side — pricing, order fulfillment, and school outreach — applying project-management and communication skills while keeping the product reliable across every delivered unit.

Aim Research Company

Manufacturing Department Intern — Summer 2025 & Summer 2026

I helped build the precision instruments that scientists rely on to detect radioactive compounds in the lab.

Aim Research Company designs laboratory equipment for HPLC and UPLC chromatography under the motto "Research, Designed Better," building instruments used in pharmaceutical research, radiochemistry, and analytical chemistry labs. As a Manufacturing Department Intern across two summers, I manufactured, soldered, and crimped production-ready hardware for two of their flagship product lines, collaborating with engineering staff on hardware integration, electrical testing, and validation.

What I worked on

  • v.ARC Model 3 — an advanced radioisotope detector for HPLC, UPLC, and other high-resolution liquid chromatography, built for detection sensitivity and resolution so researchers can identify and measure radioactive compounds during separation.
  • LCJet System Model C — an automated microplate fraction collector engineered for high-speed operation, collecting separated compounds in roughly 0.2 seconds per fraction while minimizing sample loss and cross-contamination.

Schematic & PCB design

Beyond assembly, I contributed to schematic capture and PCB layout for the LCJet control electronics alongside my engineering mentor — working in Altium Designer across the instrument's I/O, microcontroller, power supply, and motor/dryer control subsystems.

Growth across two summers

Returned for a second consecutive summer, taking on greater independence in assembly, testing, and documentation in a high-volume manufacturing environment — sharpening precision manufacturing and quality-assurance skills across both terms.

05

Passive PoE Injector Board

In Design

Independent Project — Schematic & PCB Design (Altium)

One Ethernet cable, two jobs: carry the data and carry the power.

Designed a custom Power-over-Ethernet (PoE) injector board so a single Ethernet run can both carry network data and power a downstream Raspberry Pi and PoE-capable radio equipment — useful anywhere running separate power and data lines isn't practical. Designed the full schematic and PCB layout in Altium; the board is designed and not yet fabricated.

How it works

  • The Ethernet data pairs pass straight through from the IN jack to the OUT jack, so the board is transparent to normal network traffic.
  • A Wago terminal block injects DC power (VCC and GND) onto the spare conductor pairs, riding alongside the data on the same cable to power the Raspberry Pi or radio at the other end.

Status

Schematic and PCB layout are complete; the board has not yet been fabricated or tested. Next step is ordering the board and validating the power injection under real load.

06

Oscilloscope Practice — Optical Sensor PCB

Independent Project — Test & Measurement

Before you can debug a circuit, you have to trust your scope — so I practiced the fundamentals on a real board.

Practiced oscilloscope fundamentals by probing a small custom optical sensor PCB (OSH Park–fabricated), using its onboard test point (TP1) to observe the board's output signal.

How I tested it

Identified the power and ground leads on the board's connector, powered it at 3.3V, then connected the scope's ground clip to the board's GND and probed TP1 directly. Adjusted volts/div and coupling settings to read the signal.

Result

Measured a steady DC voltage at TP1 with no AC ripple or periodic component, indicating the sensor circuit was outputting a stable bias level under static conditions rather than a dynamic signal. This confirmed correct power delivery to the board and gave hands-on practice with basic scope setup — probing, grounding, and DC voltage measurement.

Next steps

  • Try AC coupling and increase vertical sensitivity (mV/div) — a real signal riding on a DC offset can look flat under DC coupling and normal sensitivity.
  • Since it's an optical sensor, block/unblock the light path (or wave a hand near it) while watching TP1 for any change.

08

SAR ADC

In Design

Successive Approximation Register A/D Converter — Independent Project, Mixed-Signal IC Design

One comparator, one DAC, and a binary search — SAR ADCs hit research-grade resolution without an analog IC's usual power budget.

Designing an 8-bit, 10 MS/s SAR ADC for low-power sensor and IoT applications, combining a charge-redistribution capacitor DAC, a dynamic comparator, and digital SAR control logic to convert an analog input into an 8-bit code — targeting under 2 mW of power and better than 6.8 effective bits of resolution.

8-bit
Resolution, 10 MS/s target sample rate
<2 mW
Target power budget
>6.8 ENOB
Target effective number of bits

How it works

  • Each conversion samples the input, then performs a binary search: the SAR logic tests one bit at a time, the comparator checks it against a DAC-generated reference, and the bit is kept or cleared based on the result — resolving all 8 bits in 8 clock cycles.
  • The capacitor DAC (CDAC) does double duty as both the input sampler and the reference generator, which is what keeps a SAR ADC to a single comparator instead of the many a flash ADC needs.

Design considerations

  • Comparator offset/noise and CDAC capacitor mismatch are the two biggest limits on resolution and linearity — addressed with a common-centroid capacitor layout and a margined dynamic comparator.
  • Switching scheme (monotonic vs. conventional) and a bootstrapped sampling switch are chosen to minimize switching energy and avoid signal-dependent distortion at higher input frequencies.

Status

Currently working on algorithmic/behavioral modeling (MATLAB/Python) ahead of circuit-level design in the target PDK; verification plan (DNL/INL, SNDR/ENOB, Walden FoM benchmarking) is defined and will run alongside layout.
